what: International Seaways owns oil tankers. Its fleet carries crude oil and refined products across the world's oceans, chartered to oil companies and traders either for single voyages at spot rates or under time charters lasting months or years.
customers: Oil majors, national oil companies and commodity traders needing to move crude oil or refined products between continents.
money: Very large crude carriers and Suezmax vessels carrying crude oil.
Smaller vessels carrying refined products such as diesel and jet fuel.
moat: Tanker rates depend on the balance between the number of ships and the distance oil must travel, and the order book for new tankers has been very low for years — shipyards have been full of container ships and gas carriers instead. That means supply cannot respond quickly if demand for tonne-miles rises, which is the setup for very high rates.
risks: Tanker rates are among the most volatile prices in any industry: revenue went from $272.5M in 2021 to $1.1B in 2023 and back to $843.3M in 2025.
A single year's earnings tell you nothing about the next one — these are not earnings that can be extrapolated.
Last year's net margin was 36.7%, which looks wonderful and is a cyclical peak figure rather than a normal one.
Only six analysts cover the stock, so the $131.33 average target rests on thin coverage.
Oil demand growth is slowing structurally as vehicles electrify, which over decades reduces the tonne-miles to be carried.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 4.6 times earnings, 4.2 times EV/EBITDA and 6.3 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $795.9M against a $5.0B market value is a very high yield.
Debt of $576.2M against $166.9M of cash is modest for a shipping company, which historically is where they fail.
The order book for new tankers is very low, so supply cannot respond quickly to higher demand.
Longer voyage distances — oil travelling further because of trade rerouting — raise tonne-miles without any growth in oil demand.
watch: Daily charter rates and fleet utilisation. A tanker owner earns the day rate multiplied by days employed, and the rate is reported weekly.
view: Tanker shipping is the most cyclical business most investors will ever look at, and the revenue record makes the point better than any description: $272 million in 2021, $1.1 billion in 2023, $843 million in 2025. The ships did not change. Charter rates moved, and because the cost of owning a ship is largely fixed, the entire swing landed in profit. Anyone valuing this on a price/earnings ratio is capitalising a number that will be different next year.

What matters instead is the supply side, and it is genuinely favourable. Almost no new tankers have been ordered for years, because shipyards were full of container ships and gas carriers and because nobody wants to order a twenty-year asset into an uncertain oil demand future. New ships take three years to build. So if demand for tonne-miles rises, supply cannot respond, and rates spike. That is the structural case and it is the only thing worth forming a view on.

The tonne-mile point deserves explanation because it is the subtlety people miss. What matters is not how much oil the world consumes but how far it travels. When trade patterns reroute — Russian crude going to India instead of Europe, European refineries sourcing from further away — the same barrels require far more ship days. Tanker demand can rise while oil demand is flat, purely because the voyages got longer.

The balance sheet is the reassuring part: $576 million of debt against $167 million of cash is modest for shipping, which is historically where these companies die — they borrow against ships at the top of the cycle and cannot service it at the bottom. At 4.2 times EV/EBITDA and a very high free cash flow yield, you are being paid well. The long-term structural risk is electrification slowly reducing the oil that needs moving, and that is a decades-long erosion rather than a near-term threat. Day rates are the number; everything else is commentary.
bull: Longer voyage distances and a near-empty order book keep tanker rates high, and a modestly leveraged owner converts it to an enormous free cash flow yield.
bear: Rates revert as trade patterns normalise, peak-cycle earnings prove unrepeatable, and electrification slowly erodes the oil that needs carrying.
